title: Monopoly Round-Up: What Happens When Cybersecurity is Bad for Business
author: Lee Hepner
content:
Lots of monopoly-related news this week, as usual. The AI bubble continues to
blow off steam, as even Elon Musk is saying the
[neoclouds](https://www.thebignewsletter.com/p/monopoly-round-up-the-
cockroaches) are going bust, which BIG
[predicted](https://www.thebignewsletter.com/p/monopoly-round-up-the-
cockroaches) a couple of weeks ago. And, as we race toward a consequential
midterm election, Republican voters are demanding financial services reform,
and a new Congressional report called "[Settling for
Less](https://www.warren.senate.gov/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Settling-for-
Less-Warren-10.20.26.pdf)" is laying the foundation for oversight and
accountability regarding the Trump Administration's failed approach to
antitrust enforcement.

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!f4cw!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fbab2f1cd-e955-4cd6-8808-3610dac287b6_1320x1563.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!f4cw!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fbab2f1cd-e955-4cd6-8808-3610dac287b6_1320x1563.png)

But before we get to all of that, which is below for paid subscribers, you may
have seen a lot of chatter last week about a wave of AI-enabled cybersecurity
failures that resulted in the preemptive takedown of government websites
around the world. The effects were also local and diffuse. I was talking about
this with a friend who said the platform for coordinating his kid's soccer
league was shut down for a couple of days, leaving parents in the lurch on
upcoming schedules.

Basically, the internet is being ruined by a massive new AI-fueled set of
hacks, a situation nicknamed "Black October" by cybersecurity experts. Big or
small, there's a lot to unpack here and an opportunity to reflect on what this
says about our failure to anticipate and govern for risk. Let's dive in.

### A Cybersecurity Comeuppance

The situation we're dealing with is not just a few more hacks here or there,
but a step change in the vulnerability of _everything._ In the first six
months of 2026, there were 3,494 successful cyber-attacks on financial
institutions; and 16 hospitals in England shut down all non-critical
operations because of a ransomware hack. Cybersecurity "may very well be the
biggest threat to the U.S. financial system," wrote JP Morgan CEO Jamie Dimon
to shareholders.

The driver of the vulnerabilities is that AI systems make it so much easier to
hack, lowering the cost for criminals and saboteurs to go after vulnerable
systems. As cybersecurity expert Matthew Green [put
it](https://x.com/matthew_d_green/status/2110809902168031233), "We're in the
part of the movie where you need to throw whatever you can in the path of the
zombies and hope it slows them down." But just as important as the
vulnerabilities, is the heated rhetoric around them, which are disguising the
role of finance in helping to create the problem.

First, let's get to why these hacks are different. The most notable
penetration was of a web development tool called PHP, a server-side language
used by roughly 70% of the world's websites. The hacking of PHP is not a hack
of a single service or a corporate network, it's systemic. Now there is a
mechanism for a large swath of people to go after hundreds of thousands or
millions of institutions. As cybersecurity firm Wiz
[wrote](https://www.wiz.io/blog/php2shell-php-rce), "Successful exploitation
could allow attackers to take control of affected servers, steal sensitive
data, and deface the websites running on them."

I'm not a technologist, but a friend of mine provided a useful analogy: If you
think of the internet as a restaurant, your browser is like the dining room, a
server is like the kitchen that receives and sends out your order, there's a
pantry that's basically a database with all sorts of sensitive info, and PHP
is the chef that takes the order, mixes the ingredients, and sends out your
meal. And when agents can exploit vulnerabilities in PHP and essentially take
over its operations, it can throw the kitchen into chaos and start sending out
very wrong orders.

It's not just PHP, multiple core tools on top of which the internet is built
are being poked full of holes. Here's [Jason
Koebler](https://www.404media.co/php2shell-black-october-ai-is-changing-
everything-about-hacking-no-one-knows-what-happens-next/) of 404 Media:

> In the last few days, major vulnerabilities or issues have been found in
> [eMudhra](https://scotthelme.co.uk/eight-bits-of-trust-emudhras-ca-keys-
> cracked-in-milliseconds/?ref=404media.co) (an Indian entity that provides
> website security certificates),
> [Node.js](https://cybernews.com/security/php-node-js-vulnerabilities-patch-
> exploit/?ref=404media.co) (an alternative to PHP),
> [Gitlab](https://thehackernews.com/2026/10/critical-gitlab-flaw-
> cvss-100-could.html?ref=404media.co) (a software development platform),
> [Plex](https://arstechnica.com/security/2026/10/recently-fixed-plex-media-
> vulnerabilities-are-being-exploited-to-install-malware/?ref=404media.co)
> (media server software), [Railway](https://blog.railway.com/p/security-
> disclosure-wednesday-october-21st?ref=404media.co) (a cloud provider),
> [OpenCode](https://techcrunch.com/2026/10/19/hackers-hit-ai-coding-tool-
> opencode-running-up-charges-on-users-ai-accounts/?ref=404media.co) (a coding
> agent platform), and several other companies and services, though,
> rightfully, none of these has gotten as much attention as the
> vulnerabilities in PHP, called PHP2Shell, which researchers [from
> Wiz](https://www.wiz.io/blog/php2shell-php-rce?ref=404media.co),
> [Calif](https://calif.io/php2shell/?ref=404media.co), and
> [OpenAI](https://openai.com/index/coordinated-disclosure-of-critical-
> vulnerabilities/?ref=404media.co) discovered using AI.

The National Security Agency and equivalent national security agencies around
the world have encouraged organizations to take certain websites offline while
they patch them, which the governments of Germany, France, Australia,
Netherlands, Japan, the United Kingdom have done.

Although I'm skeptical of catastrophizing about AI harms, this one is very
real and bad. Aside from the ominous Black October label, the chief security
officer at Anthropic is
[warning](https://x.com/JasonDClinton/status/2090543566682718542?s=20) of a
"vulnerability tsunami," adding, "there won't be enough time to patch critical
infrastructure." _Critical infrastructure._ OpenAI CEO Sam Altman
[joined](https://x.com/unusual_whales/status/2113645872743407861?s=20) the
concern chorus, stating, "I no longer think we're going to be able to patch
all the bugs."

### Private Equity Offshored Our Software Security

And yet, there's an important context here, and one that most of the people
reporting breathlessly on Black October are leaving out. And that is, our
cybersecurity regulatory model has been a deep structural risk for a really
long time.

To make that point, I'll note that I was actually lying in the first paragraph
of this article. I wrote that there were 3,494 successful cyber-attacks on
financial institutions in the first six months of 2026. Actually, that was the
number in [the first six months
](https://www.nytimes.com/2019/07/30/business/bank-hacks-capital-one.html)_[of
2019](https://www.nytimes.com/2019/07/30/business/bank-hacks-capital-
one.html)_. UK [hospitals shutting
down](https://www.theverge.com/2017/5/12/15630354/nhs-hospitals-ransomware-
hack-wannacry-bitcoin), and of the quote from Jamie Dimon about cybersecurity
being the biggest risk to our financial system, those also took place in 2019.
S _even years ago._

Indeed, two years before that, in 2017, nearly a decade ago, hackers took
control of Dallas's [tornado warning
system](https://www.nytimes.com/2017/04/08/us/dallas-emergency-sirens-
hacking.html) and just kept waking people up.

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!7bwW!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F4223c73f-a258-4489-9fa5-c31431e58c5e_600x436.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!7bwW!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F4223c73f-a258-4489-9fa5-c31431e58c5e_600x436.png)

Why does the longstanding nature of this problem matter? Well, because if the
cybersecurity crisis existed before generative AI, then new AI hacking tools
are not the sole driver of what's going on.

A different narrative is as follows: The problem isn't just that AI has made
it easier to hack. It's that Wall Street forces the use of software that is
easy to hack because poorly written software is more profitable to sell.

Take a recent [legal
story](https://www.womblebonddickinson.com/us/insights/insights/102nfyh/unprecedented-
private-equity-firm-potentially-on-hook-for-portfolio-companys-da) about
private equity firm Bain Capital. The company bought a company, PowerSchool,
which had a severe and costly data breach. Bain, of course, had directed
PowerSchool "to offshore cybersecurity, engineering, and IT functions to
contractors," which led to "data-management tools that enabled vendors to
bypass consent protocols and access protected school district computers
directly." So there we go. Is the issue the savviness of hackers, or the
business model of private equity?

Everyone in software knows the most profitable business model is to buy a
company and slash spending on security. BIG has covered this dynamic [since
2020](https://www.thebignewsletter.com/p/another-day-another-hack-via-a-
private), and the story is always the same. There's a big hack, the reason is
some sort of giant merger, followed by cuts to security and quality control
spending, or offshoring. It became so routine BIG stopped writing about it.

For instance, there was "PE-owned SolarWinds that [let
hackers](https://mattstoller.substack.com/p/how-to-get-rich-sabotaging-
nuclear) break in to large companies and the Federal government, including our
nuclear weapons facilities," as well as "PE-owned Pulse Connect Secure [that
let hackers](https://mattstoller.substack.com/p/private-equity-barons-
responsible) take over New York subway systems," and then PE-owned software
firm Keseya, that cut R&D, offshored its software and testing development to
Belarus, responsible for a major set of randomware attacks.

These stories are so common, and happen among big companies as well, like
[Microsoft](https://www.thebignewsletter.com/p/does-microsoft-have-a-
boeing-737) or health insurers. Change Health, a United Health group company
that was the lifeblood of medical payments, got
[hacked](https://www.thebignewsletter.com/p/an-assassin-showed-just-how-angry)
in 2024, meaning that doctors, hospitals, and pharmacies were starved of
revenue for over a month. Similarly, it became impossible to buy a car in 2024
for a few weeks because of a randomware attack on the awful car dealer
software monopolist CDK Global, which BIG
[covered](https://www.thebignewsletter.com/p/a-supreme-court-justice-is-why-
you). Both Change and CDK are merger and antitrust stories.

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!pqX7!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fd8dc9878-99aa-42c2-9436-d1a37788e4f9_818x551.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!pqX7!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fd8dc9878-99aa-42c2-9436-d1a37788e4f9_818x551.png)

Major corporations from Twitter/X to Equifax to Uber have variously slashed
their cybersecurity teams, removed cybersecurity evaluations from executive
bonus compensation, and concealed evidence of massive data breaches. In 2016,
Uber suffered a data breach involving 57 million users and 600,000 driver's
licenses. Rather than alert regulators, Uber's chief security officer arranged
a payment of $100,000 to hackers to keep news of the breach from regulators
and users. He was ultimately convicted by a jury of obstructing justice and
sentenced to three years probation.

Cybersecurity [expert Bruce
Schneier](https://www.nytimes.com/2021/02/23/opinion/solarwinds-hack.html) in
2021 laid out why corporations enable this fraud with weak cybersecurity
controls. Their customers, he argued, just can't tell the difference, until
they are hacked.

> The market encourages companies to make decisions in their private interest,
> even if that imperils the broader interests of society. [So] companies… save
> money by taking on greater risk and then pass off that risk to the rest of
> us, as individuals and as a nation.
>
> The only way to force companies to provide safety and security features for
> customers and users is with government intervention. Companies need to pay
> the true costs of their insecurities, through a combination of laws,
> regulations and legal liability. Governments routinely legislate safety --
> pollution standards, automobile seatbelts, lead-free gasoline, food service
> regulations. We need to do the same with cybersecurity: The federal
> government should set minimum security standards for software and software
> development.

Schneier was right then, and he's right now. There are all sorts of contexts
in which we decide that some degree of mandatory government oversight is in
the public's best interest. Recently, a friend of mine got a new hot water
heater installed in his house, and the city inspected it to ensure it was
safe. Similarly, no one can just build a bridge based on vibes, civil
engineering is a discipline with credentials, inspections, and a dense set of
rules. As a result, no one is afraid of bridges or buildings falling down, and
when it happens, it's a really big deal. The Miami Beach Surfside building
collapse is still major news, five years after it occurred.

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!tJzo!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F50340bda-4a82-4c93-a643-297552ebefe5_625x358.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!tJzo!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F50340bda-4a82-4c93-a643-297552ebefe5_625x358.png)

That's because these are systems that were organized before neoliberalism,
when we governed and assessed risk. So the rules are clear and make sense, and
the public expects well-structured engineering.

But after the 1980s, we mostly stopped managing risk, so when Bain Capital cut
quality assurance for cybersecurity infrastructure that is equally important,
no one bothered to report on it. When the hack happened, it barely made the
papers. The cybersecurity crisis taking place this week didn't come out of
nowhere, it is the result of a deliberate _choice_ not to manage risk and the
resulting public expectations that hacks and scams cannot be reduced.

### What If Bridges Constantly Fell Down?

One reason the "AI is magic" narrative should be understood as half the story
is because cybersecurity experts have been warning for decades of the problems
created by building a society on top of bad sloppy code. Even the current
problem shouldn't be a surprise; experts have been warning about PHP
vulnerabilities since the [early
2000s](https://www.php.net/releases/4_2_2.php). The vulnerabilities at the
source of this week's cybersecurity chaos were
[identified](https://thephp.foundation/blog/2026/10/21/todays-php-security-
release-and-how-were-strengthening-php-security/) by researchers in 2024, then
disregarded because the technology didn't exist to make them exploitable.
Well, now they are.

For decades, intelligent policymakers who saw the risks of vulnerable software
sought to mandate corporate America patch its spaghetti-like IT systems, which
have been made worse by endless merger waves in which operational problems got
compounded. They also wanted the NSA to focus on defensive work instead of
stockpiling hacks to use against foreign adversaries.

But that didn't happen; the regulatory history on cybersecurity is exactly
what you'd expect in an era when we refuse public utility rules on the
powerful. Attempts to establish binding cybersecurity laws at the federal
level have been prevented through the effective lobbying efforts of industry
trade groups, and a broad lack of interest from progressives. For example, in
2013, [Congress failed](https://www.politico.com/story/2013/10/cybersecurity-
reform-going-nowhere-fast-098027) to pass comprehensive cybersecurity
legislation. So President Obama
[issued](https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-
office/2013/02/12/executive-order-improving-critical-infrastructure-
cybersecurity) an executive order called "Improving Critical Infrastructure
Cybersecurity," which directed federal regulators to survey existing
cybersecurity requirements and for the National Institute of Standards and
Technology, or NIST, to develop a cybersecurity framework in collaboration
with the private sector.

But the industry, fearing the project would result in _mandatory_
cybersecurity regulations, emphasized the adequacy of existing cybersecurity
systems. So, in 2014, when NIST issued its [Framework
1.0](https://www.nist.gov/system/files/documents/cyberframework/cybersecurity-
framework-021214.pdf), it established guidance that was _entirely voluntary_.
The Information Technology Industry Council (ITI), which represents pretty
much [every major tech company](https://www.itic.org/about/membership/iti-
members) under the sun, publicly supported the framework but continued to
lobby against any further development of mandatory regulations.
Unsurprisingly, when Congress finally passed the Cybersecurity Act of 2015, it
maintained a voluntary cyber-threat information sharing framework. And in
2016, when the FCC adopted new mandatory rules, Congress responded by
repealing them.

As of October 2026, the debate over a comprehensive, binding cybersecurity
framework rages on. Congress enacted the Cyber Incident Reporting for Critical
Infrastructure Act in 2022, requiring CISA to establish reporting rules for
covered cyber incidents and ransom payments. It was hailed as an "[important
milestone](https://www.cisa.gov/topics/cyber-threats-and-
advisories/information-sharing/cyber-incident-reporting-critical-
infrastructure-act-2022-circia)." Four years later, the final rule remains
[under review](https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news-features/us-
critical-infrastructure-circia/).

That's not to say that companies can't be held accountable, and on Friday,
former FTC Chair Lina Khan weighed in with a statement far more forceful than
anyone currently in government.

But of course, Khan has been an outlier, and certainly no one fears any
enforcement from the Trump administration along these lines.

I haven't given a comprehensive review of the policy problem, but you get the
point. What is effectively a public utility-style regulatory of core
infrastructure has been off the table since business software went mainstream
in the 1980s. And now we're reaping the whirlwind.

### Office Space

There's a pattern here that serves as a referendum on the pursuit of quick
financial gains at the expense of taking steps to safeguard the public. And
that's no different with this AI crisis. What's happened is the concerns of IT
professionals, like those of all workers, have been marginalized for decades
because addressing those concerns is bad for finance.

Among the many tech voices speaking up right now are researchers at a company
called Wiz, which referred to this week's events as "among the most severe
vulnerabilities discovered in PHP, and arguably in software history." Wiz was
acquired by Google earlier this year for $32 billion, and while it continues
to provide service to other Big Tech companies, the effect of coming under the
Alphabet umbrella is that Google now bottlenecks cybersecurity for much of the
internet.

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!AjEG!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fbucketeer-e05bbc84-baa3-437e-9518-adb32be77984.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F2543b36c-6e07-4f95-b762-e40389df3c10_1200x650.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!AjEG!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fbucketeer-e05bbc84-baa3-437e-9518-adb32be77984.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F2543b36c-6e07-4f95-b762-e40389df3c10_1200x650.jpeg)Pictured
here are consultants that Google brought in to Wiz to find out what you do
here.

So yes, AI has made hacking a lot easier, and that's a crisis. It may indeed
destroy some parts of the internet. But if we had an institutional
infrastructure where we could govern and manage risk, we might be able to get
a hold on it. Maybe the crisis will actually force such a reckoning. I mean,
the CEO of Hugging Face, which was the hack that kicked off the current
discourse, has
[encouraged](https://x.com/ClementDelangue/status/2099858032951791721) real
cybersecurity regulation.

All that said, whatever happens with AI, realize there is no addressing
cybersecurity without spending more money on risk management, which means
lowering returns on capital across corporate America. And that's the real
problem that no one in Silicon Valley or Wall Street wants to admit.

Now, on to the Good and Bad news of the week, including a penalty for Meta
that even Mark Zuckerberg might notice, a huge surveillance pricing merger
involving one of the largest advertising holding companies in the world, and a
merger that could result in an $824 billion payday for the richest man in the
world.
